  "text": "Literary scholarship inherited two uneven gifts from an early positivist influence. The first, a free‑of‑cost method, is still used to fix texts and to judge the facts gathered by literary history. The second is the notion that literature could be studied as a science, side by side with the natural sciences as imagined at the end of the 1800s. A defensive backlash began with the rise of a movement that emphasized symbols and personal imagination, rejecting the scientific dogma in favor of dream, whim, and pure pleasure, while still acknowledging that truth can be sorrowful, a view that had been voiced by a notable 19th‑century thinker. This melancholy seeped into the later emphasis on impression, where artists claimed only the surface and the fleeting, leaving deeper analysis to serious scholars. Subsequent modern poets launched harsher attacks on literary positivism, arguing that the so‑called scientific approach ignores the lived experience of creation. They also dismantled the myth of a carefree fable‑writer, showing that his work was far from simple and that any apparent distraction was only from the viewpoint of non‑artists. Critics, therefore, must keep their focus sharply on the work itself."
